scores.justification: Turn 1 labels the idea 'the electron was already in one definite state... is a common misconception,' so it notices the student is wrong, but the diagnosis is muddled and partly self-contradictory: it conflates the +x state with the z-superposition, says 'before measurement there's a 50% chance of being either spin-up or spin-down' (which IS the ignorance framing), and never isolates the actual QM5 confusion (superposition vs hidden value). Identifies wrongness but misframes the specific misconception.

Essentially no scaffolding: every tutor turn is a long lecture (coin/superposition, then Shor's algorithm, double-slit, BB84, teleportation) with at most a perfunctory 'Does this help?' at the end. No genuine eliciting questions, no use of the discriminating x-measurement. By mid-conversation the student is leading and the tutor is just affirming/expanding tangents. Information dump.

The tutor tells everything immediately and exhaustively from turn 1, including full canned explanations of collapse, qubits, and cryptography. There is no productive struggle and no withholding of conclusions at any point.

Concepts are delivered as isolated, memorizable assertions and a sprawl of unrelated applications (QKD, teleportation, Shor) that never cohere into a transferable model of the specific superposition-vs-hidden-value distinction. The boundary-condition lever (certain x vs random z) is never built; the relevance to THIS problem is lost in tangents.

On the transfer (turn 8) the tutor gives wrong physics ('When we measure the x-axis, the electron has a 50% chance of being either up or down') and tangled logic ('if there were a definitive up/down value along z, we'd expect an equal probability of measuring spin-up or spin-down along x'). The student then concludes the x-measurement gives '50% up, 50% down... no hidden value' and re-applies the everything-is-50/50 symmetry of the original misconception. The certainty of the x-result is never recognized; transfer fails.

Multiple incorrect-physics moves that reinforce/introduce misconceptions: claims the +x state measured along x is 50/50 (false; it is certain), frames pre-measurement state as a 50% 'chance of being either' (the ignorance picture), and asserts measuring one slit 'doesn't affect the other electrons' / muddled entanglement claims. The load-bearing fact is taught wrong, so this is active pedagogical harm.
